subject: Agriculture
title: The Bengal Famine of 1943
description: One-minute skill: The Bengal Famine of 1943.

hook.text: Three million people died in Bengal in 1943—not because there wasn't enough food, but because of policy.

buildup.text: British wartime policies diverted rice to military supply. Prices spiked beyond what ordinary people could pay.

discovery.text: Economist Amartya Sen showed that most famines aren't about food shortage—they're about access and power.

twist.text: Bengal actually had enough food to feed its population. Distribution failures and hoarding caused the deaths.

climax.text: The Bengal Famine shaped India's post-independence obsession with food self-sufficiency—driving Green Revolution adoption.

punchline.text: Famine can happen with full granaries. Access kills, not scarcity.

quiz.question: What did Amartya Sen conclude about the Bengal Famine?
options: Food was available but access and distribution failures caused the famine

details.summary: The Bengal Famine of 1943 killed an estimated 2-3 million people in British India, caused by a combination of wartime disruption, rice crop disease, hoarding, and colonial mismanagement. It demonstrated how political failure can turn crop stress into mass starvation.
details.whyItMatters: The Bengal Famine showed that famine is as much a political and economic failure as an agricultural one. It influenced post-independence India's commitment to food self-sufficiency that would later drive adoption of Green Revolution technologies.
takeaways: The 1943 Bengal Famine killed 2-3 million people from starvation and disease
Causes included rice crop failure, wartime disruption, hoarding, and colonial policy
The famine motivated independent India's pursuit of agricultural self-sufficiency

faq.question: What caused the Bengal Famine of 1943?
faq.answer: A cyclone and flooding damaged the rice crop. Japanese occupation of Burma cut off rice imports. British wartime policies diverted food supplies and destroyed boats to prevent Japanese advance. Hoarding and speculation drove prices beyond the reach of the poor.

faq.question: How did the Bengal Famine influence India's agricultural policy?
faq.answer: The famine's trauma drove independent India to pursue food self-sufficiency as a national security priority. This commitment led India to eagerly adopt Green Revolution technology in the 1960s, investing heavily in high-yield wheat and rice varieties to ensure the country would never face famine.
